title: Trump Signs H-1B Proclamation Requiring $100,000 Payment for Certain New Petitions
description_short: Proclamation 10973 conditioned entry for certain H-1B workers on a $100,000 payment; the requirement began September 21, 2025, with exceptions.
description_medium: On September 19, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, restricting entry of certain H-1B workers unless a $100,000 payment accompanied the petition. It took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21. Employers had to obtain and retain proof of payment before filing petitions for workers outside the United States; the Homeland Security secretary could grant national-interest exceptions. White House guidance said it covered new petitions and did not change renewal fees.
description_long: On September 19, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.” It restricted entry to the United States for certain H-1B specialty-occupation workers unless a $100,000 payment accompanied or supplemented the petition. The Homeland Security secretary could exempt an individual, a company’s workers, or an industry’s workers when hiring served the national interest and posed no threat to U.S. security or welfare. The proclamation took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2025, and set an initial 12-month term absent extension. It directed employers to obtain and retain proof of payment before filing petitions for workers outside the United States, and assigned payment verification and implementation roles to the State and Homeland Security departments. The White House FAQ said the payment applied to new petitions submitted after the effective time, not previously issued visas or earlier petitions, and did not change renewal fees. The cited material documents the policy’s terms; it does not establish any later extension or its measured effects.

title: Nine States Had Rejected DOJ Voter-Data Lawsuits by June 2026
description_short: AP reported that courts in nine states had rejected DOJ lawsuits seeking detailed voter-registration data, including Maryland.
description_medium: On June 23, 2026, the Associated Press reported that U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher dismissed the Justice Department’s suit seeking Maryland’s detailed voter records. Gallagher wrote that the state’s unredacted voter file was not a record it had to provide under federal civil-rights law. AP said similar court losses then stood at nine states and that the department had sued in 30 states and the District of Columbia.
description_long: The Associated Press reported on June 23, 2026, that U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher dismissed the Justice Department’s suit seeking Maryland’s detailed voter-registration records. Gallagher, appointed by President Donald Trump during his first term, wrote that she “joins every court to have addressed this issue” in concluding that the unredacted voter file was not a record Maryland had to produce to the United States. The Justice Department relied on an opinion from its Office of Legal Counsel asserting a right to the data under federal civil-rights law; Gallagher wrote that the court would not interpret the Civil Rights Act contrary to its text simply because the office advancing that view had adopted it. AP said the records sought included dates of birth, addresses, driver’s-license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. It reported that Maryland brought the number of states where courts had rejected similar demands to nine, and that DOJ had sued in 30 states and the District of Columbia. The AP report also identified similar rulings in Arizona, California, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Oregon, Rhode Island and Wisconsin. It described a Georgia dismissal as based on filing in the wrong city, after which DOJ refiled elsewhere.

prior_source_fact_map.quote: U.S. District Court Judge Stephanie Gallagher last week dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit against Maryland that sought access to the state’s voter records.

Gallagher, appointed by Republican President Donald Trump during his first term, wrote that she “joins every court to have addressed this issue” in concluding that the unredacted voter registration file “is not a record or paper that a state must produce to the United States.”

The department has sued to force release of detailed state voter data — which includes dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — in 30 states and the District of Columbia.

In the Maryland case, the Justice Department tried to cite an opinion written by its own legal counsel’s office that it had the right to the state voter records under federal civil rights law, but Gallagher was not persuaded.
“The Court will not interpret the (Civil Rights Act) contrary to its text simply because an office of the party advancing that interpretation has adopted it,” she wrote.
With the dismissal Thursday in Maryland, the number of states where the Justice Department has lost similar cases comes to nine.
In addition to Maryland, judges have rejected those attempts in Arizona, California, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Oregon, Rhode Island and Wisconsin.
In Georgia, a judge dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit because it had been filed in the wrong city, prompting the government to refile elsewhere.

title: Trump’s Hormuz Warship Demand Met No Immediate Allied Commitment
description_short: AP reported on March 18, 2026, that Trump was demanding allied warships to unblock the Strait of Hormuz; no close ally had offered immediate help.
description_medium: An Associated Press report published March 18, 2026, said President Donald Trump was demanding allied warships to help unblock the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. It reported no close ally had offered immediate help. Keir Starmer said Britain would not be drawn into the wider war without international-law backing and a considered plan; Germany’s defense minister opposed sending more ships, while France said possible escorts would wait until fighting subsided.
description_long:
Associated Press reporters John Leicester and Emma Burrows reported on March 18, 2026, that President Donald Trump was demanding allied warships to help the United States unblock the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. The report said no close ally had offered immediate help.

British Prime Minister Keir Starmer said Britain would not be drawn into the wider war without international-law backing and a “proper thought-through plan.” The report said the United Kingdom first refused use of its bases for U.S. attacks on Iran, then accepted their use for strikes on Iran’s ballistic-missile program. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the war was not Germany’s and that more warships would not advance diplomacy. French President Emmanuel Macron said France was not taking part and described possible Strait escorts only after fighting subsided. French military spokesman Col. Guillaume Vernet said any escort mission would depend on talks with Iran.

AP described the refusals as evidence of limited European goodwill, but did not measure a lasting change in U.S. standing.

title: Court Orders Trump to Pay $2 Million for Trump Foundation Misuse
description_short: A November 2019 court order required Trump to pay $2 million after misuse of Trump Foundation funds for his political interests.
description_medium: On November 7, 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced a court order requiring Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for misuse of Trump Foundation assets during the 2016 campaign. Trump admitted misusing charitable funds. Settlements also imposed restrictions on future charitable service and directed the dissolved Foundation’s remaining assets to independent charities.
description_long:
On November 7, 2019, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced that the New York Supreme Court had ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million in damages for improperly using charitable assets to advance his political interests during the 2016 presidential primaries. The order formed part of the resolution of the state’s lawsuit against the Trump Foundation and its directors.

Trump admitted personally misusing Foundation funds. The admissions included allowing his campaign to control the timing, amounts and recipients of approximately $2.8 million raised through a January 2016 veterans fundraiser. He also admitted using charitable money to settle obligations of companies he controlled and purchasing a $10,000 portrait with Foundation funds.

The Foundation had agreed to dissolve under court supervision in December 2018. The resolution directed its remaining $1.78 million in assets and Trump’s damages payment to eight independent charities. It required training for the Trump children and imposed restrictions on Trump’s future charitable service, including independent oversight and a five-year reporting requirement if he formed a new charity.
